description: We are a team of five passionate STEM students working on PyreSync, a geospatial platform that harmonizes NASA MODIS and VIIRS active fire data to analyze historical fire activity and detect unusual seasonal patterns. We are interested in GIS, satellite data, environmental science, and software development. We're looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in Python, GIS, data analysis, frontend development, or scientific research who are excited to build impactful solutions using NASA data.
summary:
PyroLens is a satellite-based project that helps people understand fire activity across the Nile Delta. It uses NASA FIRMS data from MODIS and VIIRS to explore active-fire detections over time and across different locations.

The project turns satellite data into clear maps and visual information, making it easier to explore fire patterns and notice unusual changes. It also provides access to historical records and the latest available detections through an interactive website.

We created PyroLens to make satellite data easier to understand and more accessible and to support environmental monitoring and research in an important agricultural region of Egypt.
details:
PyroLens: Wildfire Intelligence for the Nile Delta

1. Our Main Goal

When we started working on this project, we wanted to do more than just show fire locations on a map. We wanted to find a way to understand how fire activity changes over time and whether some periods show unusual patterns.

One challenge we noticed is that MODIS and VIIRS do not detect fires in exactly the same way. They have different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities, which makes comparing their raw detection counts difficult.

So, our main focus was to build a more consistent way to organize and compare this data. We worked on cleaning the records, reducing duplicate detections, accounting for differences between the two satellite instruments, and using statistical methods to identify unusual activity.

The result is a dataset covering around 26 years, from 2000 to 2026, with 57,358 processed records. We made this data available through an interactive website where users can explore the results instead of having to process the satellite data themselves.

2. The Problem

The Nile Delta is an important agricultural and populated area in Egypt. Fire activity in this region can affect crops, land, nearby communities, and air quality.

However, understanding whether fire activity is increasing or becoming unusual is not always easy. NASA provides fire detections from different satellites, but these satellites do not collect data in exactly the same way.

MODIS has been collecting data since 2000, with a resolution of around 1 km. VIIRS started later, in 2012, and has a finer resolution of around 375 m. This means VIIRS can detect smaller fires that MODIS might miss.

Because of this difference, simply comparing the number of detections from different years can give misleading results. A sudden increase in detections after 2012, for example, does not always mean that there were actually more fires. It may partly be caused by the change in satellite technology.

There are also differences in how the two instruments report confidence levels, and the same fire may be detected by both satellites, which can lead to double counting.

We wanted to deal with these problems and make the data more consistent, easier to compare, and easier for people to explore.

3. How PyroLens Works

PyroLens combines a historical dataset with a live data update system.

First, we collected NASA FIRMS data from MODIS and VIIRS. We then used a Python pipeline to organize the data and make it more suitable for comparison.

The main steps are:

  • Data cleaning: We organized the data into a common format and converted timestamps to UTC.
  • Grid system: We placed detections on a shared 1 km grid so that data from the two instruments could be compared more consistently.
  • Filtering: We used a static-source and offshore mask to remove detections that are not likely to represent vegetation fires.
  • Removing duplicates: Detections in the same grid cell on the same day are counted as one event, even if more than one satellite detected them.
  • Sensor adjustment: We calculated a monthly adjustment factor using the period when MODIS and VIIRS data overlap. This helps make the historical record more comparable over time.

After processing, the data is used to create three main products:

  • hotspots.geojson, which contains the fire locations and their information.
  • calendar.json, which stores monthly fire activity.
  • anomalies.json, which contains the monthly statistics used to identify unusual activity.

For anomaly detection, we use median and MAD-based robust z-scores. This helps us compare each month with its usual historical pattern and identify periods with unusually high or low activity.

4. The Website

We built an interactive website so users can explore the results without needing to download or process the original data themselves.

The website includes:

  • An interactive map showing fire detections across the Nile Delta.
  • Different map backgrounds, including satellite imagery and a dark map style.
  • Filters for date range, satellite, confidence level, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).
  • Information about each detection, such as its location, date, satellite, confidence, and FRP.
  • A monthly anomaly heatmap that helps users see which months had unusual fire activity.
  • A live mode that shows the latest available detections.
  • A data update indicator that tells users when new data has been published.

Users can select a month from the heatmap and view the related detections on the map. This makes it easier to move between the statistical results and the actual locations.

5. Technologies and Tools

We used different tools to build the data pipeline and the website.

For data processing, we used Python, pandas, and PyArrow to clean and organize the historical dataset. We also used Node.js scripts to prepare the data products and update the live data.

For the website, we used TypeScript, Leaflet, Tailwind CSS, and Vite. Leaflet handles the interactive map, while Tailwind CSS helps with the website design.

We used NASA FIRMS as the main source of fire detections. The live update system uses GitHub Actions to check for new data every hour, process it, and publish the updated website through GitHub Pages.

During development, we also used AI-assisted support for some coding and troubleshooting tasks. The team made the main project decisions and reviewed the implementation.

6. What Makes Our Project Different?

One of the main things that makes PyroLens different is that it does not only display fire locations. It also tries to make data from different satellite instruments more comparable.

Instead of using a simple count of all detections, we process the data, remove duplicates, and adjust for differences between MODIS and VIIRS. We also use statistical methods to identify unusual activity instead of relying only on visual changes in the number of detections.

Another important part is the live update system. The website is not just a fixed map or a collection of old data. It checks NASA FIRMS regularly and updates the available information automatically.

We also wanted the project to be accessible. That is why we built it as a free website that does not require users to install special software or have experience working with satellite data.

7. Benefits and Expected Impact

PyroLens can help different groups understand fire activity in the Nile Delta.

Researchers and students can use the platform to explore historical patterns and work with organized fire data. Environmental researchers can use the monthly statistics to study unusual periods and compare different years.

Agricultural and local decision-makers may use the information to better understand where and when fire activity is happening. The platform can also help people become more aware of environmental changes in the region.

Our project is designed as a monitoring and analysis tool. It does not replace official emergency systems or confirm the cause of every fire detection.

8. Limitations

There are some limitations that users should keep in mind.

First, satellite detections are not always confirmed fires. They can include other heat sources, so the results should be treated as active-fire detections rather than confirmed wildfire events.

Also, near-real-time data is not instantaneous. NASA FIRMS data depends on satellite passes and data processing, so there can be a delay before new detections appear on the website.

Finally, our definition of an event is based on a 1 km grid cell during one day. This is useful for organizing and comparing the data, but it does not mean that every event represents one separate physical fire.

We included these limitations because we want users to understand what the data can and cannot tell them.

9. Conclusion

With PyroLens, we wanted to make NASA satellite fire data easier to explore and more useful for understanding fire activity in the Nile Delta.

By combining historical data, statistical analysis, an interactive map, and automatic updates, the platform gives users a clearer way to explore where and when fire activity is unusual.

PyroLens is free, accessible, and open-source (source code: https://github.com/tokka252-tech/pyrolens/), and we hope its approach can be adapted to other regions in the future.
